title: Mr. G, Your Lesson Sucks!
author: Golazeski, Daniel
summary: Golazeski recounts a student, Terry, telling him after three days of geometry rotation lessons that he still 'wasn't getting it' — which Golazeski hears not as a complaint about the lesson but as the student quietly asking whether he's stupid. The piece's real argument is that a student's confusion is diagnostic information the teacher is obligated to act on, not a fixed trait of the student. His practical fix has two parts: a differentiation move that avoids public labeling (framing independent-vs-group work as a 'preference,' not a leveled sorting), and a genuine pedagogical discovery — having students draw one small directional-arrow diagram before each rotation problem — that only surfaced because he kept trying after his existing method failed for one student. The essay closes by generalizing from the anecdote: a lesson doesn't need a dramatic overhaul to fix confusion, and giving students permission to say 'this isn't working' is what makes teachers find those small, high-leverage adjustments at all.
points: A student saying 'I'm not getting this' after genuine effort should be heard as 'am I stupid?' — a call to change the teaching, not the student.
Framing a differentiation choice as 'work independently or with me' rather than 'advanced vs. remedial group' removes the public stigma of being sorted by ability.
A single small diagram (drawing rotation direction as an arrow before each problem) was the missing piece that made an already-decent method work.
One student's willingness to admit confusion improved the lesson for every student taught after him.
The adjustment that finally worked was minor and specific, reinforcing the claim that fixing confusion rarely requires reinventing the whole lesson.
quotes: Students who say, "I hate math!" usually mean, "I hate feeling stupid!" This article explores one way to turn our classrooms into a place where students feel smart.
When a student like that tells me they're not understanding a topic after three days, I don't know any other way to hear that except, "Mr. G, your lessons suck!

I said, "Thank you for telling me. If a student like you is struggling with this topic, then I need to figure out a better way of teaching it." Terry smiled and walked out of my room confident that I would come up with a way to help.

The question wasn't "Are you good or bad at rotations?" it was "How would you prefer to work today?" It became a choice of working independently versus collaboratively. No one had to openly admit to the entire class that they were still confused about rotations.
That small diagram helped Terry see how the cardinal directions change during a rotation, and everything else fell into place.

If Terry hadn't asked for help, and if I hadn't pushed myself to try to be better than what I thought was my best, I never would have found this piece of the puzzle. All of the students I taught after Terry benefited from his willingness to admit that my lesson wasn't working for him.
